name: pointread
_comment: Why is BF only at parity on skewed point reads, when that is the paper's
headline (~2x)?  Three things about how we measure, each of which suppresses
the effect, and none of which is a property of the fork:
1. THE CACHE WAS NEARLY EMPTY.  read_big cached 17,373 records in a 128 MiB
ring that holds ~970,000 at 138 B/record -- 1.8% full.  A single-threaded
20 s run touches ~187k rows and promotes 5% of them.  The advantage IS
holding the hot set, so a run that never fills the cache cannot show it.
Fix: long warmup, and measure the hit rate, not just ops/s.
2. PROMOTION RATE 5% vs the reference's 30% (../bf-tree/benchmark/
bench_bftree.toml, storage benchmark; 100% for its in-memory one).
3. THE OS PAGE CACHE DWARFED THE ENGINE.  memmax 1G with a 256M budget
leaves ~700 MiB of page cache -- 2.7x the engine budget, and page-
granular, which is precisely the tier the paper removes with direct I/O.
We cannot do direct I/O here, but memmax 384M leaves ~100 MiB, so the
engine's own cache is the cache.
The arithmetic that says the win should be there, at a 256 MiB budget:
BF holds ~970k hot rows in the ring; stock holds 64k pages, and under a
scattered zipf each cached page carries ~1 useful hot row, so ~64k rows.
~15x more hot rows cached for the same bytes.  If a saturated cache still
does not beat stock, THAT is a finding about the integration.

experiments.name: saturated_skew
_why: 120 s of warmup before the 60 s measurement, so the ring is full
rather than 1.8% full.  Read cached_records and rec hit% first:
if they are still small, the run is still too short.

experiments.name: promotion_rate
_why: Ours defaults to 5%, the reference uses 30%.  If 30 is much
better than 5, the default is simply mistuned.

experiments.name: page_cache_pressure
_why: The control for gap 3: the same comparison with the roomy cgroup
the earlier campaigns used.  If BF wins at 384M and not at 1G,
the OS page cache was hiding the effect, not the fork.
